1. Forest Areas and Wildlife
Continued preservation of the tropical forests in the present Canal Zone and their wildlife is one of the key elements of the environment which will be affected by the proposed Treaty. As noted earlier, because of restrictions on public access to the Canal Zone watershed and defense areas, much of the Zone is now an island of forest in the midst of a generally cleared country-side, which has helped preserve a wide variety of birds and animals. For these reasons, the future of these forests is ecologically important. Tracts of particular concern are the Canal Zone Forest and Wildlife Preserve (Madden Forest), Barro Colorado Island, the Pipeline Road area near Gamboa, and the Fort Sherman-San Larenzo-Achiote Road area.
The proposed Treaty will affect these areas as follows:
-- Madden Forest Reserve will be incorporated into the Panamanian park system, according to RENARE officials.
-- Barro Colorado Island in Gatun Lake is the site of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute. It is presently a U.S. Government Federal Reserve. The Institute has a contract with the Panamanian Government Ministry of Health signed in January 1977 which covers its research operation throughout Panama. Barro Colorado and the Institute's other holdings will be the subject of separate international agreements with the Republic of Panama. Three peninsulas opposite the Island are held by the Institute under license from the Canal Zone Government. These areas will continue under the Canal Commission's control and this should continue to afford protection to the Island and its habitat.
